message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

The cost table is arithmetically correct, and the pilot data are a real asset. But the document misreads its own pilot results, uses a participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data, and overlooks a treatment capacity limit that it states itself. Once these are corrected, the service is **not fully funded** by the provisional allocation, and the case for a single uniform service doesn't hold. Several of the author's claims depend directly on these errors.

## 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types

Table 1 shows:

| | Participation | Food waste per participating household |
|---|---|---|
| Houses | **66%** | 1.9 kg |
| Flats | **21%** | 1.4 kg |

Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses, and those that took part produced less. This is the opposite of what section 2, section 7 and the author's summary claim.

The conclusion drawn from it, to roll out uniformly "without a separate approach for flats", is therefore unsupported. Low participation from flats is a well-known problem: communal bins, limited storage, and no obvious place to put an outdoor caddy. The pilot suggests Thornbury has the same problem. About 10,400 households, 20% of the district, are flats, so a flat-specific approach should be planned for, not ruled out.

## 2. The 64% participation rate doesn't come from the pilot

Section 3 applies a "pilot's 64% participation rate", but the pilot shows **57% overall** and **66% for houses**. There is no 64%.

Since the pilot had the same share of flats as the district (20%), the straightforward projection is by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **≈2,870** |

The study projects 3,290 tonnes, which overstates tonnage by about **15%**.

Two further cautions:
- Six-month pilots usually benefit from novelty and close attention. Participation often falls once a service becomes routine, so even 2,870 t may be optimistic.
- Table 1 measures *average weekly set-out*, which is usually lower than participation as normally defined: setting out at least once in a period. The study uses the two terms interchangeably. It should define which one it means and use that consistently.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Section 4 states that Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Both projections exceed this:

| | Projected | Over capacity |
|---|---|---|
| Study's figure | 3,290 t | ≈1,490 t |
| Corrected figure | ≈2,870 t | ≈1,070 t |

This changes the finances:
- **The disposal saving is capped.** 1,800 t × £74 = **£133,200**, not £243,000, unless the surplus can be treated elsewhere at a similar cost.
- **The surplus has to go somewhere.** The next AD plant is **46 miles** away: a 92-mile round trip compared with 28 miles for Brookfield. That adds haulage cost, a gate fee the study doesn't state, and vehicle time. Six vehicles planned around a 14-mile trip may not be able to absorb it, which could mean more vehicles or a transfer arrangement.
- The author's statement that "treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the tonnage until 2029.

The study's own numbers show this. It isn't an external objection.

## 4. The service is not "fully funded"

| | Study | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Annual cost | £733,400 | £733,400 + unlisted costs |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ≈£133,200 (capped) |
| **Net cost** | **≈£490,000** | **≈£600,000+** |
| Provisional allocation | £520,000 | £520,000 |
| **Position** | £30,000 surplus | **≥£80,000 shortfall** |

The corrected net cost of £600,000 *before* treating the surplus ~1,070 t at the 46-mile plant.

Further points on funding:
- The allocation is **provisional**, and the government has "indicated" funding rather than confirmed it. Its duration, and whether it continues beyond the first years, isn't stated. Calling the service "fully funded" overstates the certainty even before the shortfall.
- **The cost table may be incomplete.** The author says "every cost line is shown", but the table lacks:
  - cover for sickness and holiday,
  - a spare vehicle (six vehicles with no reserve),
  - supervision and management,
  - the dedicated phone line and web page from section 6,
  - recruitment and training,
  - haulage of the surplus tonnage.
- **No round analysis.** Six vehicles serving 52,000 households means about 8,700 households per vehicle per week, about 1,730 a day. That's demanding for a two-person crew. The study should show the round modelling, or the pilot's own productivity figures, to support it.

The table's own arithmetic is correct: vehicles £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400, crews £408,000, total £733,400.

## 5. Other evidence points

- **Satisfaction (81%):** The study doesn't give the sample size or the response rate. If the people who responded were mainly participants, which seems likely given only 21% of flats took part, the figure probably overstates satisfaction among all households.
- **Contamination under 2%:** This is a good result. Give the number of spot checks so readers can judge how robust it is.
- **Seasonality:** The pilot ran January–June. Food waste yields vary through the year, so a note on this would help.

## 6. Implementation timetable

The timeline is very tight and has no contingency:
- **Vehicles:** ordered by December, delivered in March, collections from 5 April. Any delay in vehicle delivery delays the launch. What's the fallback, for example short-term hire?
- **Caddies:** delivering to **52,000 households** in March is a major logistics exercise. The study gives no procurement lead time or delivery plan.
- **Crews:** recruited from February and trained in March, which leaves almost no margin if recruitment is slow.
- **Cabinet approval** has to come before the December order, so the decision is needed in the next few weeks.

## Author's description compared with the document

| Author's claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| Participation "held up across houses and flats" | 66% compared with 21% |
| Single uniform service justified | Pilot suggests flats need a different approach |
| Projections based on pilot behaviour | Uses 64%, which isn't in the pilot data (pilot: 57%) |
| "Treatment is local" | Only for 1,800 t; the rest has to go 46 miles |
| Net cost ≈£490,000, "fully covered" | ≈£600,000+ against a provisional £520,000 |
| "Every cost line is shown" | Cover, spares, management, helpline and haulage missing |
| "Timetable works back from vehicle lead time" | Yes, but with no contingency |

## Recommendations

1. Correct section 2 to say that participation from flats was much lower, and plan a specific approach for flats, such as communal bins, different caddies or targeted engagement.
2. Re-project tonnage by housing type (about 2,870 t), with a lower-participation sensitivity case.
3. Address the Brookfield capacity limit. Either negotiate more capacity, or cost the 46-mile option, including the effect on vehicle numbers. Recalculate the disposal saving accordingly.
4. Complete the cost table and restate the net cost against the allocation, showing the funding gap and how it would be met.
5. Describe the funding as provisional, with its expected duration.
6. Add contingency plans for vehicle delivery, caddy logistics and recruitment.

Because the service is a statutory requirement, Cabinet is effectively deciding how to deliver it, not whether to. That makes an accurate picture of the funding gap and the flats problem more important, not less. The pilot is a strong foundation, and a corrected study would give Cabinet a sound basis for the decision.
